performers: Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Frederick Stock; Walter P. Zimmerman, organ
recorded: 22 December 1926, Orchestra Hall, Chicago; issued by Victor in July 1927
intro: Elgar’s Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 in D, Op. 39, played by the Chicago Symphony under Frederick Stock, with Walter P. Zimmerman at the organ. The organ enters at the return of the trio tune.

sections.label: Intro · Off-beat opening in E♭
sections.mNote: A forceful opening in E♭ before the move to D major.

sections.label: A · Strings begin the quick march
B · Trio in G major
sections.mNote: Violins, clarinets and horns play the tune.

sections.label: A′ · Return of the quick march
sections.mNote: The short string phrases return in D major.

sections.label: B′ · Trio theme in D major, with organ
sections.mNote: The trio theme returns in D major over organ pedals.

sections.label: Coda · Running strings and wind phrases
sections.mNote: Running strings and short wind phrases close the march.

cues.title: Chicago recording, 1926
cues.text: On 22 December 1926 Frederick Stock and the Chicago Symphony recorded the march for Victor in Orchestra Hall, with Walter P. Zimmerman at the organ. Victor made four takes. The third was issued.
cues.evidence: Victor recording ledger, matrix CVE-37282, reproduced by the Discography of American Historical Recordings: personnel, venue, four takes and take 3 as master. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800011535

cues.title: String melody and bass, rehearsal A
cues.text: At rehearsal A the strings play two firm accents beside a quick run of notes. The bass has a figure of its own, sometimes dissonant against the tune above. The passage, in D, is marked Allegro, con molto fuoco.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal A, p. 130 in this reprint: string melody and bass figure. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6e/IMSLP24159-PMLP23738-Elgar_-_Pomp_and_Circumstance%2C_Op._39%2C_No._1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First trio, G major
cues.text: The first trio is in G major. Four horns play the long tune with the first violins and clarinets, and the bassoons and lower strings play an even accompaniment. Elgar marks the melody legato e cantabile.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal I, Trio, p. 138 in the linked reprint: first violins, two clarinets and four horns share the melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: American première, Chicago, 1902
cues.text: Theodore Thomas conducted the American première of the march with the Chicago Orchestra at the Auditorium on 28 November 1902. In 1926 Stock took the same orchestra into the recording session heard here.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society dates the US première to 28 November 1902, with Theodore Thomas and the Chicago Orchestra: https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-b.htm. Stock’s 1926 session is documented in DAHR matrix CVE-37282.

cues.title: Return of the trio, organ pedals
cues.text: The trio returns in D major, marked Molto maestoso. Elgar wrote the organ part for pedals alone at first, specifying sixteen- and thirty-two-foot stops. Zimmerman’s hands join later on the manuals, adding chords as the tune continues.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, after rehearsal R and at S. The organ part specifies pedals only, 16 and 32 feet, before the manuals enter: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e7/IMSLP50146-PMLP23738-Elgar-PompCirc1.Organ.pdf. DAHR identifies Zimmerman.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda
cues.text: After the great tune, Elgar returns to quick notes. The strings play running figures and the woodwinds exchange short phrases. The march ends with a clipped accent and a held D, and the organ pedals join the final chord.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal T to the end, pp. 153–154 in the linked reprint; organ part, final pedal note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
